Ohio statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit above $50 or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater, bears 5% annual interest on the excess if tenant stays six months or more. (R.C. 5321.16(A); source)
  • Deductions must be itemized in a written notice delivered with the amount due within thirty days after termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession. (R.C. 5321.16(B); source)
  • If the landlord fails to comply, tenant may recover the money due plus damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld and reasonable attorney fees. (R.C. 5321.16(C); source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy may be ended by landlord or tenant on notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date. (R.C. 5321.17(B); source)
  • Landlord must comply with applicable building, housing, health and safety codes and make repairs to keep premises fit and habitable. (R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2); source)
  • Landlord must give reasonable notice before entering; twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable. (R.C. 5321.04(A)(8); source)
  • Landlord may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession because of tenant's protected acts. (R.C. 5321.02(A); source)

Which rentals does Ohio landlord-tenant law cover?

Chapter 5321 of the Revised Code governs residential rentals across Ohio, and R.C. 5321.01 defines the terms. A tenant is a person entitled under a rental agreement to use and occupy residential premises to the exclusion of others. A landlord can be the owner, lessor or sublessor, an agent, or anyone authorized to manage the premises or collect rent. A rental agreement can be written or oral.

The chapter carves out several kinds of occupancy, including hospitals and care homes, hotels, motels and similar transient lodging, boarding school housing, farm residences tied to renting at least two acres of farmland, and an owner living in a condominium unit. A landlord selling a house that is rented out should confirm the arrangement is a true residential tenancy before relying on the chapter's rules.

The chapter also takes away local control of rents. Under R.C. 5321.19, no city, county or township may impose rent control or rent stabilization or otherwise regulate rights and obligations the chapter already covers. Local building, housing, health and safety codes stay in force, and so do rent rules for housing the local government itself owns.

What must an Ohio landlord do to keep a rental fit to live in?

The duties are listed in R.C. 5321.04. A landlord who is a party to a rental agreement must:

  • Follow building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety.
  • Repair what is broken and do whatever is reasonably needed to keep the unit livable.
  • Keep common areas safe and sanitary.
  • Keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning fixtures and appliances that the landlord supplies in good working order.
  • Supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required to have them or the tenant controls the system.
  • Provide waste receptacles and removal when the landlord has agreements covering four or more units in one structure.

Entry has its own rule. Except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable, the landlord gives reasonable notice and enters at reasonable times, and twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable. A landlord who enters improperly, or demands entry so often that it harasses the tenant, can owe the tenant proven losses and legal fees, and the tenant may seek an injunction or walk away from the agreement.

Because these duties attach to the landlord, they matter to a person who is thinking of selling a rental in poor shape. Unfixed code problems can lead to a tenant's remedies before the sale closes.

How do Ohio security deposits work?

The deposit rules are in R.C. 5321.16. A deposit above fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater, earns five percent annual interest on the excess if the tenant stays six months or more. The landlord figures and pays that interest once a year.

When the tenancy ends, the landlord may apply the deposit to past due rent and to damages caused by the tenant's breach of the rental agreement or of the tenant's statutory duties. Every deduction must be itemized in a written notice delivered with the amount owed, within a month of the day the agreement ends and the keys come back.

The tenant has a job too. The tenant must give the landlord a forwarding address in writing. Without one, the tenant cannot collect damages or attorney's fees if the landlord mishandles the deposit. If the landlord does fail to comply, the tenant may recover the money due, damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees.

What notice ends an Ohio tenancy, and what notice starts an eviction?

Ending a periodic tenancy and starting an eviction are separate steps. Under R.C. 5321.17, either side can end a weekly rental on a week's notice, and a rental that renews monthly on notice that reaches the other side a full thirty days ahead.

An eviction action under Chapter 1923 begins with a different notice. R.C. 1923.04 requires the party seeking possession to tell the other to leave three or more days before filing, by certified mail with return receipt, by handing a written copy to the defendant, or by leaving it at the usual home or the premises. A landlord's notice must carry this wording, printed or written conspicuously: 'You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance.'

One narrow case moves faster. If a landlord has actual knowledge or reasonable cause to believe a tenant or household member has engaged in a violation described in R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i), the landlord gives a three-day termination notice and then promptly files an action under Chapter 1923 if the tenant stays.

What can an Ohio tenant do about repairs, retaliation or a lockout?

Three protections come up most often.

  • Repairs. Under R.C. 5321.07, a tenant sends written notice naming the problem to the place rent is normally paid. When the problem outlasts a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever comes first, and rent is paid up, the tenant may pay rent into the municipal or county court, petition for a repair order, or terminate the agreement.
  • Retaliation. Under R.C. 5321.02, raising rent, trimming services, or filing or threatening an eviction is barred when the cause is a tenant's report of a code violation to a government agency, a habitability complaint to the landlord, or collective bargaining with other tenants.
  • Self-help. Under R.C. 5321.15, a landlord may not cut off utilities, lock a tenant out, or threaten unlawful acts to recover possession, and may not seize a tenant's belongings for rent without a court order. A landlord who does so owes all damages caused plus attorney's fees.

Landlords whose agreements cover three or fewer dwelling units, and who said so in writing, are outside the rent-deposit remedy, as are student tenants in college-owned housing. A small landlord should check that exception before assuming it covers their situation.

Which statutory points should a landlord check before selling an Ohio rental?

Landlord and tenant periods in the Ohio Revised Code, as the statute text states them
SubjectPeriod or amountSection
Deposit itemization and refundOne month from the end of the agreement and handover of possession5321.16(B)
Interest on large depositsFive percent annually on the part above $50 or one month's rent, once the tenant has stayed six months5321.16(A)
Ending a monthly rentalThirty days before rent is next due5321.17(B)
Ending a weekly rentalA week's notice5321.17(A)
Notice to leave before an eviction filing3 or more days1923.04(A)
Entry notice presumed reasonable24 hours5321.04(A)(8)
Repair cure window before tenant remediesReasonable time or 30 days, whichever is sooner5321.07(B)

Before listing a tenant-occupied house, a seller should gather the written lease, the rent ledger and the deposit records, and put one question to the closing agent: how do the lease and the held deposit pass to a buyer? Some owners tired of repairs and turnover choose a direct as-is purchase of the house while a tenant lives there.

More questions about Ohio Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What notice ends a monthly rental in Ohio?

Thirty days before rent is next due. A weekly rental needs seven days before the date it ends. R.C. 5321.17 sets both periods.

When must a deposit come back to an Ohio tenant?

Thirty days, measured from the day the lease ends and the tenant hands the unit back. Itemized deductions travel in writing with the balance. A tenant who wants the refund mailed should give a forwarding address in writing.

Can an Ohio landlord enter without permission?

Only with reasonable notice and at reasonable times, except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable. The statute presumes twenty-four hours is reasonable notice.

Can Ohio cities set rent control?

No. R.C. 5321.19 bars political subdivisions from rent control or rent stabilization on private rentals that the chapter regulates. Local housing and building codes still apply.

Can an Ohio landlord lock a tenant out over unpaid rent?

No. R.C. 5321.15 prohibits cutting off utilities, excluding a tenant from the premises, and threatening unlawful acts to recover possession outside Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. The landlord is liable for damages and attorney's fees.

Ohio law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • A month-to-month tenancy may be terminated or not renewed by notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date (no-cause). (R.C. 5321.17(B); source)
  • Landlord must promptly commence a Chapter 1923 action to remove a tenant who fails to vacate within three days after the notice required by R.C. 5321.17(C). (R.C. 5321.04(A)(9); source)

How many days of notice must an Ohio landlord give before filing an eviction?

At least three days in most cases. R.C. 1923.04 requires the party who wants possession to tell the other side to leave the premises three or more days before beginning the court action. The notice goes by certified mail with return receipt requested, by handing a written copy to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises.

When a landlord is recovering a residence, the notice must carry this statement in a conspicuous place: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." A notice without it is the first thing an owner or buyer should check.

Which other Ohio notice periods can apply?

The three-day notice is the gateway to court, but other chapters of the Revised Code set the notice that ends a tenancy in the first place. The table lists the ones that come up most when a rented house is being sold.

Ohio notice periods for ending a residential tenancy
SituationNoticeAuthority
Week-to-week tenancyAt least seven days before the termination dateR.C. 5321.17(A)
Month-to-month tenancyAt least thirty days before the periodic rental dateR.C. 5321.17(B)
Tenant fails a health and safety dutyWritten notice, ending not less than thirty days after receiptR.C. 5321.11
Drug-related violation tied to the premisesTermination three days after the notice is givenR.C. 5321.17(C)
Land installment contractNotice under R.C. 5313.06 counts as the notice to leaveR.C. 1923.04(B)

Source: Ohio Revised Code, sections cited in the table.

What notice does a landlord give when the tenant is behind on rent?

R.C. 1923.02(B) says a tenant under an oral tenancy who is in default on rent forfeits the right of occupancy, and the landlord may end the tenancy by giving the three-day notice described in R.C. 1923.04. A tenant who holds over after the term ends, or who breaches a written rental agreement, can also be sued once that notice has run.

Keep records of how and when the notice was delivered. Court clerks and judges look at the delivery method, so an owner should be able to show the certified mail receipt, the date of hand delivery, or where a copy was left.

Which special cases change the notice rules in Ohio?

A few situations carry their own delivery rules. When the person to be removed is a deceased resident of a manufactured home park, R.C. 1923.04(C) says the notice must be left at the premises and also mailed by ordinary mail to the executor or administrator if the probate court has appointed one, and to the resident's spouse and other immediate family members when the park operator knows their names and addresses.

R.C. 1923.02(C) lets a landlord end the tenancy by giving notice under R.C. 1923.04 when a resident or occupant who is on the state sex offender registry lives within one thousand feet of a school, preschool or child care center, children's crisis care facility or residential infant care center. A landlord who has that right but does not use it is not liable in damages for what happens as a result.

Student tenants of a college or university follow a separate path under R.C. 5321.031, which the eviction chapter points to. Owners with a unit of that type should read that section before serving anything.

What may an Ohio landlord not do in place of a notice?

Ohio bars self-help eviction. R.C. 5321.15 prohibits a landlord from cutting off utilities or services, excluding the tenant from the premises, or threatening an unlawful act to recover possession, except through the court process in Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. It also bars seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions to collect rent without a court order, and a landlord who breaks the rule owes the tenant all damages plus reasonable attorney fees.

R.C. 5321.02 adds a retaliation rule. A landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten a possession action because the tenant:

  • complained to a government agency about a building, housing, health or safety code violation that materially affects health and safety;
  • complained to the landlord about a violation of the landlord's duties under R.C. 5321.04;
  • joined other tenants to negotiate collectively over the rental agreement.

A tenant can use retaliation as a defense to the possession case, recover possession, or end the agreement, and can also recover actual damages and attorney fees. A rent increase that reflects the cost of improvements the landlord installed is allowed.

How does a notice affect the sale of a rented Ohio house?

It decides whether the buyer receives the house empty or with a tenant in place. An owner who wants a vacant house should serve the right notice for the tenancy type, such as the thirty-day notice for a month-to-month tenant, and then follow the court steps if the tenant stays. A buyer who is happy to keep the tenant can skip the notice and take over the lease.

Security deposits matter at closing and at move-out. Under R.C. 5321.16, a deposit above fifty dollars or one month's rent, whichever is greater, earns five percent annual interest on the excess if the tenant stays six months or more. When the tenancy ends, deductions must be itemized in a written notice delivered within thirty days after termination and delivery of possession, and the tenant must supply a forwarding address. A landlord who wrongly withholds owes the amount withheld again as damages plus attorney fees.

  • Pull the lease, ledger and any notices before listing.
  • Tell the title company where the deposit sits.
  • Decide in the contract whether the buyer takes the house vacant or tenant-occupied.

Where can an Ohio tenant or landlord get help with a notice?

Ohio Legal Help publishes a plain-language timeline that starts with the three-day notice, says to read the notice for the required sentences, and recommends trying to settle before a case is filed, with any agreement in writing. It also points to free legal services for some low-income tenants through Right to Counsel programs in Akron, Cleveland, Columbus and Toledo, and to local legal aid offices elsewhere.

Landlords can ask the clerk of the municipal or county court that covers the rental address how to file once the notice period has passed. Clerks explain forms and fees but do not give legal advice, so owners with a complicated tenancy, such as a lease with a purchase option or a mixed-use building, should speak with a landlord attorney before serving anything.

More questions about Ohio Eviction Notice Rules

Is a three-day notice in Ohio an eviction?

No. It is the required warning before a case. R.C. 1923.04 says the notice must be given three or more days before the court action begins, and only a court judgment can lead to removal by an officer.

Can an Ohio landlord change the locks or shut off the water to force a tenant out?

No. R.C. 5321.15 forbids terminating utilities or services, excluding the tenant, or threatening unlawful acts to recover possession. The landlord owes damages and attorney fees for a violation.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Ohio?

At least thirty days before the periodic rental date, under R.C. 5321.17(B). A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days before the termination date.

Does the notice have to say anything specific?

Yes. A residential notice under R.C. 1923.04 must contain the statutory statement that begins 'You are being asked to leave the premises.' It must be printed or written conspicuously.

Can I sell my rented Ohio house while a notice is pending?

Yes, an owner can contract to sell, but the tenant's right to remain follows the notice and court process. Settle in the contract who delivers possession and when, and keep copies of every notice for the buyer.
